headline: Monopoly was invented to warn against monopolies
dek: In 1904 Lizzie Magie patented a board game with a lesson built in.

slides.label: The bright idea
slides.title: A lesson you could play
slides.text: Lizzie Magie followed the economist Henry George, who argued that rent paid to landowners enriches the few and keeps tenants poor. In 1902 she described her game as a practical demonstration of the present system of land-grabbing.
slides.alt: Studio portrait of the economist Henry George, balding, with a full beard and a bow tie
slides.credit: Henry George, about 1886. Unknown photographer. New York Public Library. Public domain.

slides.label: It worked
slides.title: Patented and passed around
slides.text: She was granted a US patent on January 5, 1904. Players drew their own boards and changed the street names. A Wharton economist used it in class, and Quakers in Atlantic City played it with local streets.
slides.alt: Patent drawing of a square game board with spaces marked For Sale and For Rent, railroads, a Bank, a Public Treasury and a Go to Jail corner
slides.credit: The Landlord's Game, US patent 748,626, 1904. Lizzie J. Magie. Public domain.

slides.label: Wait, what?
slides.title: To win, get rich
slides.text: Her 1904 patent says the object of the game is to obtain as much wealth or money as possible. The lesson depended on players seeing what that did to everyone else. In 1932 she added Prosperity rules, where everyone gains when someone gets rich.

slides.label: The backfire
slides.title: Monopoly
slides.statLabel: Monopoly sets sold worldwide, Hasbro said in 2015
slides.text: In 1935 Parker Brothers began selling a version as Monopoly, bought from Charles Darrow, who claimed he invented it. Its rules: become the wealthiest player, and the last player left in the game wins. The warning became the goal.

slides.label: Could anyone have seen it coming?
slides.title: Partly
slides.text: Her own 1904 rules made getting rich the way to win, and the lesson rested on players noticing the cost. Before 1935 people were copying the board and changing its rules. A store-bought version that kept the race and dropped the argument was harder to see.

slides.label: The long cleanup
slides.title: Her name came back
slides.text: In 1935 Parker Brothers paid Magie $500 for a revised patent. By 1936 she and her anti-monopolist rules were largely forgotten. In the 1970s, research for a lawsuit over a game called Anti-Monopoly brought her patents back to light.

slides.label: The ledger
slides.title: Worth it?
gains: 275 million Monopoly sets sold worldwide, Hasbro said in 2015
A board still in use: spaces around the edge, a jail, a corner to start from (US patent 748,626, 1904)
A game economics teachers used in class decades before it hit stores
costs: A game built to criticize land monopoly, best known as a game about winning one
$500 from Parker Brothers for her patent, and decades without credit
Her anti-monopolist rules, largely forgotten by 1936
slides.text: Millions learned to play. Fewer learned what she meant. You decide if it was worth it.

slides.label: Credit for trying
slides.title: We owe her one
slides.text: Magie took on a hard problem: making an economic argument something people could feel at a kitchen table. She kept refining it, with a second patent in 1924. The board she designed is still the one families play.

slides.label: How the pattern works
slides.title: Players learn the rules
slides.text: To show the harm of land-grabbing, the game made land-grabbing the way to win. Players practiced the winning moves. The warning lived in the commentary, and the commentary did not come in the box.

slides.label: How you do this
slides.title: Your warnings flip too
slides.text: You start a channel of the worst customer emails so the team learns how not to treat people. Within a month it is the most popular channel at work, and people post the emails to laugh at the customers. The lesson flipped.
also: A biggest-bill leaderboard meant to shame waste that people try to top
A scary safety video that people quote for fun

slides.label: Lessons
slides.title: What we take from it
items: People learn what they practice, not what they are told it means.
A message that depends on its explanation can lose the explanation when it spreads.
The version that sells is not always the version that was meant.

portrait.credit: Lizzie Magie, about 1892. Unknown photographer. Public domain.
